blogs.title: When Is 'Ongoing' Enough? Farahi and the Long Shelf Life of FOIA Exemption 7(A)
blogs.description: This post would examine the D.C. Circuit’s treatment of staleness under Exemption 7(A), especially its conclusion that a terse 2023 declaration could validly 'update' much older, more detailed submissions rather than rebuild the agency’s showing from scratch. It would analyze how Farahi reads CREW, Juarez, and the requirement that enforcement proceedings be 'pending or reasonably anticipated,' and ask whether the court has effectively made it easier for agencies to preserve 7(A) withholdings in long-running investigations.

blogs.title: FOIA in the Shadow of Counterterrorism: Deference, National Security, and the FBI’s Law-Enforcement Showing
blogs.description: This post would focus on the opinion’s strong deference to the FBI on both the 'law enforcement purposes' prong and the interference prong, particularly where national security and terrorism allegations are in the background. It would explore how the court relied on Campbell, Pratt, and CNSS, and consider whether Farahi further entrenches a two-track FOIA doctrine in which ordinary law-enforcement cases and counterterrorism files receive meaningfully different judicial scrutiny.

blogs.title: Judging FOIA From Behind the Curtain: Ex Parte Declarations After Farahi
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s acceptance of sealed, ex parte declarations as central to both the Exemption 7(A) and segregability rulings. It would discuss the opinion’s waiver reasoning, the practical limits on adversarial testing in national-security FOIA litigation, and the broader institutional question whether appellate review remains sufficiently meaningful when the key justifications for withholding never enter the public record.

blogs.title: Segregability Without Disclosure: What Farahi Means for 'Meaningful Information' in Investigative Files
blogs.description: This post would unpack the court’s segregability analysis, especially its reliance on Mead Data’s idea that FOIA is about disclosing meaningful information, not isolated words or phrases scattered through exempt material. It would consider how that approach works in enormous investigative files, why the court was willing to accept the FBI’s claim that nonexempt material was too interwoven to release, and what this means for requesters challenging categorical withholdings when they cannot point to specific overbreadth.
